questions.q: Using the method 'Machine Learning Model Accuracy', work with: correct = 60, total = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of accuracy_pct.
questions.a: 30 per cent

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Machine Learning Model Accuracy' and work with: correct = 24, total = 60. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of accuracy_pct.
questions.a: 40 per cent

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Machine Learning Model Accuracy' refers to.
questions.a: Machine learning is the branch of artificial intelligence where a program builds its own model from example data instead of following hand-written rules; after training, the model is scored by the share of test cases it gets right.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Machine Learning Model Accuracy'.
questions.a: A model earns trust only when its score on unseen testing data crosses the accepted accuracy bar.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Machine Learning Model Accuracy', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: accuracy_pct = correct / total * 100

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Five Characteristics of Big Data' refers to.
questions.a: Datasets too bulky or messy for ordinary database tools are called big data; they are judged on five traits: sheer volume, speed of arrival (velocity), mix of formats (variety), trustworthiness (veracity) and the useful knowledge hidden inside (value).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Five Characteristics of Big Data'.
questions.a: Volume alone is not enough; how fast data arrives, how mixed and how reliable it is decides whether it is truly big data.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Five Characteristics of Big Data', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: judge(data) on volume, velocity, variety, veracity, value

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sizing Daily Big Data Generation' refers to.
questions.a: Web users, phones and connected gadgets produce data on a colossal scale each day; expressing the daily flood in familiar storage units shows why special processing systems are needed.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sizing Daily Big Data Generation'.
questions.a: Roughly 2.5 quintillion bytes arise every day, which is a few exabytes and far beyond a single machine.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sizing Daily Big Data Generation', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: exabytes_per_day = daily_bytes / 1024 ** 6

questions.q: Using the method 'Web of Things Single Interface', work with: apps_per_device = 5, devices = 4. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of apps_avoided.
questions.a: 19 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Web of Things Single Interface' and work with: apps_per_device = 20, devices = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of apps_avoided.
questions.a: 1999 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Web of Things Single Interface' refers to.
questions.a: The Internet of Things links everyday gadgets so they can exchange data, while its Web of Things extension lets one browser-based interface operate them all, instead of forcing a separate app for every device.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Web of Things Single Interface'.
questions.a: Moving control onto the web collapses a pile of device-specific apps into one interface.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Web of Things Single Interface', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: apps_avoided = devices * apps_per_device - 1

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sensors and Smart Cities' refers to.
questions.a: A sensor samples the physical world, such as motion, tilt or tremors, and a smart sensor adds on-board computing so it can process readings before passing them on; city infrastructure stitches such sensors into services like quake-warning buildings and self-reporting bridges.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sensors and Smart Cities'.
questions.a: Accelerometers detect orientation and gyroscopes add rotation detail, which is how a phone flips its display.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sensors and Smart Cities', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: sense(input) -> process -> alert

questions.a: 360 units

questions.a: 15000 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Pay-per-use Cloud Billing' refers to.
questions.a: Cloud computing rents software, platforms or raw infrastructure over the Internet, and providers bill usage the way an electricity board does: the longer or heavier you use a resource, the more you pay.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pay-per-use Cloud Billing'.
questions.a: On-demand billing spares a new organisation from buying servers before it earns revenue.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Pay-per-use Cloud Billing', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: monthly_cost = hours_used * rate_per_hour

questions.q: Using the method 'Grid Computing Parallel Speedup', work with: nodes = 3, task_hours = 200. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of time_saved.
Take the relation taught for 'Grid Computing Parallel Speedup' and work with: nodes = 30, task_hours = 300. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of time_saved.
questions.a: 290 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Grid Computing Parallel Speedup' refers to.
questions.a: A grid welds geographically scattered computers, called nodes, into a virtual supercomputer for one large job; splitting the job evenly lets the nodes work simultaneously, so the waiting time shrinks by roughly the node count.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Grid Computing Parallel Speedup'.
questions.a: Unlike cloud, which sells services, a grid pools volunteered nodes for a single application-specific goal.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Grid Computing Parallel Speedup', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: time_saved = task_hours - task_hours / nodes

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Blockchain Decentralised Ledger' refers to.
questions.a: A blockchain keeps one shared ledger on every participating computer instead of one central database; verified transactions are packed into blocks that append to the chain, so no single member can quietly rewrite history.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Blockchain Decentralised Ledger'.
questions.a: The append-only design means an entry becomes final only when every node authenticates it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Blockchain Decentralised Ledger', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: new_block -> all nodes verify -> chain grows
